SANDRA DINIS, ACTING WARDEN

TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE FIFTH CIRCUIT


BRIEF FOR THE RESPONDENT
SUPPORTING VACATUR


OPINIONS BELOW
The opinion of the court of appeals ( J.A. 34-36) is reported at 133 F.4th 453 .  The memorandum opinion and
order of the district court (J.A. 28-33) is available at
2023 WL 6578464 .  The report and recommendation of
the magistrate judge (J.A. 18-27) is available at 2023
WL 6635074.
JURISDICTION
The judgment of the court of appeals was entered on
April  3, 2025.  A petition for rehearing was denied on
June 23, 2025  (J.A. 37).  The petition for a writ of certiorari was filed on August 20, 2025 , and granted on June
1, 2026.  The jurisdiction of this Court rests on 28 U.S.C.
1254(1).

2

STATUTORY PROVISIONS INVOLVED
Pertinent statutory provisions are reproduced in the
appendix.  App., infra, 1a-35a.
INTRODUCTION
The Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) has long allowed some federal prisoners to serve the final stages
of their prison terms in halfway houses or home confinement in order to ease their transition back into society.
When formalizing BOP’s authority  to move a prisoner
from prison to those transitional locations  before his
term of imprisonment expire s, Congress referred to
halfway houses and home confinement as “prerelease
custody.”   18 U.S.C. 3624(c).   As relevant here, t he First
Step Act  of 2018 , Pub. L. No. 115 -391, 132 Stat. 5194 ,
enabled certain prisoners who participate in recidivism -
reduction programming to earn “time credits ” that may
then be applied to accelerate their placement in prerelease custody.   18 U.S.C. 3624(g)( 1) and (2).
Petitioner , a federal prisoner serving a 20 -year term
of imprisonment , filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. 2241 , contending that BOP had
wrongfully withheld First Step Act time credits from
him and seeking, as a remedy, that his transfer  from
prison to prerelease custody be accelerated.  The district
court dismissed that claim for failure to exhaust administrative remedies .  But the court of appeals affirmed on
the alternative ground that petitioner’s claim is not cognizable in habeas  at all  and instead should have been
brought under Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents
of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics , 403 U.S. 388 (1971) .
That reasoning is incorrect, and not just because the
potential availability of a remedy under Bivens is farfetched.  This Court’s precedents establish that habeas,
not a civil -rights suit, is the correct vehicle for a pris-

3

oner to challenge  unlawfully prolonged confinement in
prison and to seek “speedier release into the community”
—even though such a prisoner would , like someone on
parole or bail, remain in  legal custody and still be subject to significant constraints on his liberty.  Wilkinson v.
Dotson, 544 U.S. 74, 82 (2005) ; see Preiser v. Rodriguez ,
411 U.S. 475 , 487-488 (1973) (holding that habeas was
available for state prisoners ’ claims for restoration of
good-time credits, which would allow them to be transferred from prison to parole at earlier date s).
The district court’s dismissal of petitioner’s habeas
petition was nevertheless correct.  Even setting aside
the exhaustion issue  decided by the district court , petitioner’s claim is barred by 18 U.S.C. 3621(b), which the
First Step Act amended to provide that BOP’s “ designation of a place of imprisonment   * * *  is not reviewable by any court. ”  This Court’s usual practice, however,
would be to vacate the court of appeals’ judgment and
remand for consideration of those issues in the first instance by the courts below .  Alternatively, the Court
may wish to dismiss the writ of certiorari as improvidently granted because Section 3621(b) ’s review bar deprives the question presented of practical significance
and because petitioner’s own habeas petition may soon
be moot  if BOP’s own calculations of petitioner’s time
credits result in his transfer to a halfway house .
STATEMENT
Following a jury trial in the United States District
Court for the District of New Jersey, petitioner was
convicted on one count of conspiring to violate the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, in violation of 18 U.S.C. 1962(d); one count o f conspiring to
commit securities fraud, in violation of 18 U.S.C. 371;
one count of conspiring to commit wire fraud, in viola-

4

tion of 18 U.S.C. 1349; 16 counts of wire fraud, in violation of 18 U.S.C. 1343; one count of conspiring to commit
money laundering, in violation of 18 U.S.C. 1956(h); one
count of conspiring to obstruct justice, in violation of 18
U.S.C. 1512(k); and one count of conspiring to sell or
transfer a firearm to a prohibited person, in violation of
18 U.S.C. 371 and 18 U.S.C. 922(d)(1) (2006).  11 -cr-740
Judgment  1.  He was sentenced to 240 months of imprisonment, to be followed by three years of supervised release.  11-cr-740 Judgment  3-4.  The court of appeals affirmed, 41 F.4th 136, and this Court denied a petition
for a writ of certiorari, 145 S. Ct. 189.
In 2022, petitioner filed a petition for a writ of habeas
corpus under 28 U.S.C. 2241  in the Eastern District of
Texas.  J.A. 1-14.  The district court dismissed the petition.  J.A. 28-33.  The court of appeals affirmed.  J.A. 34-
36.
A. Custody Of Federal Prisoners
1. A person who is convicted of a federal crime and
sentenced to a term of imprisonment is “ committed to
the custody ” of the Bureau of Prisons , a component of
the Department of Justice,  “until the expiration of the
term imposed .”  18 U.S.C. 3621(a).   During that term,
BOP “designate [s] the place of the prisoner’s imprisonment” after considering various factors, including “the
resources of the facility contemplated ,” “the nature and
circumstances of the offense ,” “the history and characteristics of the prisoner ,” any non-binding “ recommend[ation]” by the sentencing court of “a type ” of facility as appropriate , and what facilit ies are closest to
the prisoner’s primary residence .  18 U.S.C. 3621 (b) and
(b)(1)-(4).  BOP operates the federal prisons, which are
generally classified by security level —minimum, low,

5

medium, or high.  See United States  v. Price, 84 F.4th
738, 740 n.3 (7th Cir. 2023).
Many federal prisoners , however,  do not serve their
entire terms of imprisonment in prisons.   For one thing,
prisoners can earn good -time credits b y “display[ing]
exemplary compliance with institutional disciplinary
regulations ,” 18 U.S.C. 3624(b)(1) , and those credits entitle them to earlier release.  See 18 U.S.C. 3624(a).   In
addition , some prisoners are permitted to spend the final stages of their terms in prerelease custody —which
includes transitional non -prison environments like halfway houses and home confinement.  See 18 U.S.C. 3624(c).
BOP has been placing federal prisoners in  halfway
houses and home confinement  for decades.  In the early
1960s, Attorney General Kennedy and the BOP Director decided to  open experimental halfway houses  (or
“prerelease guidance center [s]”) for juvenile offenders
in four major cities.  See Robert F. Kennedy, Halfway
Houses Pay Off , 10 Crime & Delinq. 1 , 1 (1964).  As they
do today, the halfway houses had “an informal atmosphere” and gave residents “much wider latitude than
prevails in institutions,”  but also imposed various restrictions, including curfews, prohibitions on drugs and
alcohol, and requirements  to sign in and out .  Albert J.
Riess, Jr. et al. , Treating Youth Offenders in the Community: An Account of a New Approach in Correctional Treatment Launched by the United States Bureau of Prisons in the Fall of 1961 , at 13 -14 (John J.
Galvin ed. 1966) ; see Gov’t Accountability Off ice, Bureau of Prisons: Actions Needed to Better Achieve Financial and Other Benefits of Moving Individuals to
Halfway Houses on Time  7 (2026).
In the years  that followed , BOP expanded its reliance on  halfway houses, which became more formally

6

known by terms like “residential reentry center”  (RRC)
and “community corrections facilit y.”  See 28 C.F.R.
570.20(a) (listing forms of “community confinement”) .
In 1986, the  first federal home -confinement program
was introduced as a cheaper  alternative to halfway
house s.  See Darren Gowen, Overview of the Federal
Home Confinement Program 1988 -1996, 64 Fed. Prob.
11, 11 (2000) .
Congress formalized BOP’s authority to place prisoners in prerelease custody  in the Second Chance Act
of 2007, Pub. L. No. 110 -199, § 251 (a), 122 Stat. 692-693
(2008).  The prerelease -custody provision, 18 U.S.C.
3624(c), provides that  BOP
shall, to the extent practicable,  ensure that a prisoner serving a term of imprisonment spends a portion of the final months of that term  (not to exceed
12 months) under conditions that will afford that
prisoner a reasonable opportunity to adjust to and
prepare for the reentry of that prisoner into the community.
18 U.S.C. 3624(c)(1); see 18 U.S.C. 3624(c)(1) and (2)
(providing that “prerelease custody” may include “a
community correctional facility” or “home confinement”).
A prisoner can be placed in home confinement for only
“the shorter of 10 percent of the term of imprisonment
of that prisoner or 6 months .”  18 U.S.C. 3624(c)(2).
Section 3624(c) further provides that “[n]othing in
this subsection shall be construed to limit or restrict the
authority of the Director of the Bureau of Prisons under
section 3621” to designate prisoners’ places of imprisonment.  18 U.S.C. 3624(c)(4); see 18 U.S.C. 3621.   The
Second Chance Act also amended Section 3621 to specify that a sentencing court cannot require that a prison
term be served in a halfway house.  § 251(b), 122 Stat.

7

693; see 18 U.S.C. 3621(b) (“ Any order, recommendation, or request by a sentencing court that a convicted
person serve a term of imprisonment in a community
corrections facility shall have no binding effect on the
authority of the Bureau under this section to determine
or change the p lace of imprisonment of that person. ”);
see also 18 U.S.C. 3582 (a) ( providing that the sentencing court may “ make a recommendation concerning the
type of prison facility appropriate for the defendant ”).
2. Even after a term of imprisonment ends (whether
upon release from a prison, a halfway house, or home
confinement ), many federal criminal  sentences then
provide for a term of supervised release.  See 18 U.S.C.
3583.  “ Supervised release is a form of postconfinement
monitoring that permits a defendant a kind of conditional liberty by allowing him to serve part of his sentence outside of prison, subject to conditions on his behavior.”  Esteras v. United States , 606 U.S. 185, 192
(2025) (citation s and internal quotation marks  omitted).
Congress created supervised release in 1984 to replace
most forms of federal parole, which was a similar and
longstanding form of post -imprisonment supervision.
See Johnson v. United States , 529 U.S. 694, 696-697, 710
(2000); see also Anderson v. Corall, 263 U.S. 193, 194 &
n.1 (1923) (describing the 1910 federal parole statute) .
Standard conditions of supervised release include
that the releasee “ not knowingly leave the federal judicial district where he or she is authorized to reside without first getting permission from the court or the probation officer ”; “live at a place approved by the probation officer ” and “notify the probation officer at least 10
days before [a] change” of residence; “allow the probation officer to visit   * * *  at any time ”; “work full time
(at least 30 hours per week) at a lawful type of employ-

8

ment” unless excused by probation; and several others .
Sentencing Guidelines § 5D1.3(b)(2) (2025) .  Violation of
a condition exposes the releasee to the potential revocation of supervised release and return to prison to serve
“all or part of the term of supervised release.”  18 U.S.C.
3583(e)(3).
B. The First Step Act
In 2018 , Congress passed and the President signed
the First Step Act, 132 Stat. 5194 , a “landmark  piece of
legislation” affecting the federal criminal -justice system.  Hewitt v. United States , 606 U.S. 419, 424 (2025) ;
see Pulsifer  v. United States , 601 U.S. 124, 155 (2024)
(Gorsuch, J., dissenting).   Title I of the Act, titled “Recidivism Reduction,”  132 Stat. 5195  (capitalization altered), directed the Attorney General to develop a “risk
and needs assessment system” to assess federal prisoners’ recidivism risk  and provide them with “ evidence -
based recidivism reduction programming ,” 18 U.S.C.
3632(a)(3).   That programming can include such activities as “ classes on morals or ethics ,” “cognitive behavioral treatment,” and “ faith-based classes or services ,”
among others.  18 U.S.C. 3635(3)(C)(iii), (v), and (ix).  The
Act provides prisoners with multiple incentives for successful participation, including extra phone and visitation privileges, potential transfer to a prison closer to
home, and most relevant here, the opportunity to earn
“time credits. ”  18 U.S.C. 3632( d)(1)-(4).
In general, an eligible prisoner “ earn[s] 10 days of
time credits for every 30 days of successful participation
in evidence -based recidivism reduction programming  or
productive activities .”  18 U.S.C. 3632(d)(4)(A)(i); see 18
U.S.C. 3632(d)(4)(D) (listing offenses  of conviction  that
render prisoners ineligible  for such time credits).  Those
time credits “shall be applied toward time in prerelease

9

custody or supervised release ,” to which BOP “shall
transfer eligible prisoners, as determined under [18
U.S.C.] 3624(g) .”  18 U.S.C. 3632(d)(4)(C).   Prerelease
custody based on First Step Act time credits is not subject to the time limits on such custody imposed by the
Second Chance Act.  See 18 U.S.C. 3624(c) and (g)(10).
But a prisoner can be moved to supervised release
based on such credits only up to 12 months early.  See
18 U.S.C. 3624(g)(3).
Section 3624(g) applies to a prisoner who “has earned
time credits under the risk and needs assessment system  * * *  in an amount that is equal to the remainder
of the prisoner’s imposed term of imprisonment ” and
who satisfies several other requirements, including  having been determined by BOP to pose a sufficiently low
risk of recidivism.   18 U.S.C. 3624(g) (1)(A); see 18
U.S.C. 3624 (g)(1).  When transferred to home confinement, a prisoner must generally “ be subject to 24 -hour
electronic monitoring ” and “ remain in the prisoner’s
residence ” except to engage , with BOP ’s approval,  in
activities such as going to work  or religious services ,
performing community service, receiving medical treatment, and attending important family gatherings.  18
U.S.C. 3624(g)(2)(A)(i)(I) and (II).   A prisoner who is
transferred to a halfway house is “subject to such conditions as the Director of the Bureau of Prisons determines appropriate .”  18 U.S.C. 3624(g)(2)(B) .  For prisoners transferred to home confinement or halfway
houses, BOP must, “ to the extent practicable, provide
that increasingly less restrictive conditions shall be imposed on prisoners who demonstrate continued compliance with the conditions of such prerelease custody .”  18
U.S.C. 3624(g)(4).

10

Title VI of the First Step Act also amended in two
ways Section 3621(b), the provision that gives BOP authority to designate the place of imprisonment  and precludes a sentencing court from giving “binding effect”
to any request or order that a term of imprisonment be
served “ in a community corrections facility .”  18 U.S.C.
3621(b).  First, the Act specified that BOP should , subject to considerations like “bed availability” and “the
prisoner’s security designation,” “place the prisoner in
a facility as close as practicable to the prisoner ’s primary residence .”  Ibid.; see First Step Act § 601 (1), 132
Stat. 5237 .  Second, the Act inserted a sentence at the
end of the subsection, providing that, “[n] otwithstanding any other provision of law, a designation of a place
of imprisonment under this subsection is not reviewable
by any court.”  18 U.S.C. 3621(b); see  First Step Act
§ 601(2), 132 Stat. 5237.
C. The Present Controversy
1. Petitioner is a federal prisoner serving a 20-year
sentence for his role in a criminal scheme to take over
FirstPlus  Financial Group, Inc., a Texas -based mortgage-loan company, and to drain FirstPlus of its assets.
41 F.4th at 157 -162, 165.
In 2007, petitioner, who was an attorney, conspired
with members of La Cosa Nostra to take over FirstPlus
because it was “receiving periodic, multi -million-dollar
‘waterfall’ payments from its bankruptcy trust .”  41
F.4th at 158; see id. at 159.  Petitioner and one of his co -
conspirators sent letters to FirstPlus’s  CEO and other
members of its board of directors threatening to report
the company to federal agencies for “financial misconduct including bribery, money laundering, and Sarbanes-Oxley [Act] violations,” as well as  to tell the
CEO’s wife that the CEO  “had raped an assistant and

11

used the company ’s moneys to pay off the victim when
she got pregnant .”  Id. at 159.
After the CEO met with petitioner and petitioner’s
co-conspirator, the CEO  persuaded the board to step
down and a new board  was assembled , with petitioner’s
brother as CEO.  41 F.4th at 159.  Petitioner became the
company’s “special counsel,” which enabled him to facilitate arrangements whereby money flowed out of First-
Plus to his co -conspirators in the guise of payments for
consulting services.  Id. at 160 (citation omitted) .  Petitioner and his confederates “bled FirstPlus dry,” draining the company of more than $14 million and leaving it
with “less than $2,000” in its accounts.  Id. at 162, 165.
Petitioner also conspired to transfer a firearm to two
co-conspirators who were convicted felons.  See id. at
196-197; see also 18 U.S.C. 922( d)(1).
In 2011, a federal grand jury in the District of New
Jersey returned a 25-count indictment against petitioner
and 12 other defendants.  11 -cr-740 Indictment .  Petitioner was charged with conspiring to violate RICO;
conspiring to make false statements in connection with
a loan application; conspiring to commit securities
fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, and bank fraud;
wire fraud; conspiring to obstruct justice; and conspiring to transfer a firearm to a prohibited person.  Id. at
2-78, 82-87.
A jury found petitioner guilty on all counts except
conspiring to commit bank fraud and to make false
statements.  41 F.4th at 165 & n.13; 11 -cr-740 Judgment
1.  The district court sentenced petitioner to 20 years  of
imprisonment, to be followed by three years of supervised release.  11-cr-740 Judgment  3-4.  The court of appeals affirmed, 41 F.4th 136, and this Court denied a petition for a writ of certiorari, 145 S.  Ct. 189.

12

2. In 2022, petitioner filed a  pro se petition for a writ
of habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. 2241 in the Eastern
District of Texas, the district where he is imprisoned .
J.A. 1-14.  The petition alleged in relevant part  that
BOP had unlawfully failed to “consider” transferring
petitioner  to prerelease custody  based on his First Step
Act time credits and the “[18 U.S.C.] §  3621(b) factors.”
J.A. 10; see D. Ct. Doc. 1 -1, at 41 (Feb. 7, 2022) ( petitioner’s supporting memorandum , stating that he “seeks
earned time credits toward RRC and home confinement
under the First Step Act (for which [petitioner] has
earned between 42 and 48 months [of ] time credits )”).
A magistrate judge recommended that the habeas
petition  be dismissed .  J.A. 18-27.  The magistrate judge
found that petitioner had failed to exhaust administrative remedies on his First Step Act claim .  J.A. 24 (finding “no records” establishing exhaustion) .  She further
concluded that petitioner’s  other claim , involving provisions of the  Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act  (CARES Act) , Pub. L. No. 116 -136, 134 Stat.
281 (2020), that had expanded access to  home confinement, failed on the merits .  J.A. 25-26.
The district court adopted the magistrate judge’s
recommendation and dismissed the habeas petition.  J.A.
28-33.  It agreed that petitioner had failed to exhaust
his First Step Act claim, stating that petitioner “was
clearly challenging the BOP’s refusal to grant him his
requested relief of home confinement ,” yet “[n]one of
[his administrative] grievances mention the entitlement
to FSA earned time credits as authority for why [p]etitioner should now be placed in home confinement or a
halfway house.”   J.A. 31.  The court likewise  agreed that
petitioner’s CARES Act  claim was meritless .  J.A. 32.

13

3. The court of appeals affirmed  on other grounds .
J.A. 34-36.  It noted its previous holding that “ a habeas
petition ‘is the proper vehicle to seek release from custody,’ while a civil rights suit under Bivens v.  Six Unknown Named Agents of Fed. Bureau of Narcotics , 403
U.S. 388  (1971), is the ‘proper vehicle to attack unconstitutional conditions of confinement and prison procedures.’ ”  J.A. 35 (quoting Melot v. Bergami , 970 F.3d
596, 599 (5th Cir. 2020)) ; but see J.A. 35 n.1 ( noting a
contrary nonprecedential Fifth Circuit decision) .  The
court then stated that “ the nature of [petitioner’s]  requested relief is transfer to a halfway house or home
confinement .”  J.A. 35.  Because “neither form of relief
would entitle him to accelerated release, ” the court reasoned, “the relief he seeks is properly brought in a civil
rights suit ” rather than in habeas.  Ibid.
The court of appeals thus did not address “whether
[petitioner] sufficiently exhausted his administrative
remedies because, even if he did, § 2241 is not the proper
vehicle.”  J.A. 35.  The court also noted that petitioner
had waived his CARES Act claim  on appeal.  J.A. 35 n.1.
4. When petitioner sought this Court’s review, the
government acknowledged that there is “language in
this Court’s opinion in Jones v. Hendrix, 599 U.S. 465
(2023),” that is “inconsistent” with the conclusion that a
prisoner cannot use a habeas petition to “challenge
BOP’s execution of time credits under the First Step
Act” “solely because application of those credits would
not accelerate his release from custody.”  Br. in Opp. 8.
But the government opposed certiorari, in part because
petitioner had “failed to exhaust administrati ve remedies” for his claim about First Step Act time credits .
Ibid.

14

This Court granted review on its own statement of
the first question  presented  in the petition for a writ of
certiorari , and later appointed an amicus curiae to support the judgment below.
5. BOP has informed this Office that , under BOP’s
most recent “FSA Time Credit Assessment” for
petitioner —completed on July 25, 2026 —petitioner has
earned 1275 days of First Step Act time credits , which
means that he is projected , contingent on his good behavior,  to become eligible for transfer to a halfway
house on January 22, 2027.   The same projected eligibility date was provided to petitioner at his most recent
inmate “program review ” in June 2026.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
A prisoner’s claim alleging the unlawful withholding
of First Step Act time credits and seeking accelerated
transfer to a halfway house or home confinement  is cognizable in habeas.
A. Although the scope of habeas corpus was narrower
at the Founding, it has evolved to serve as the remedy
for a prisoner who alleges “that he is being unlawfully
subjected to physical restraint ” and seeks “to obtain release from such confinement .”  Preiser v. Rodriguez, 411
U.S. 475, 486 (1973); see id. at 485.  In a line of precedent
starting with  Preiser, this Court has elucidated which
types of prisoner claims must be brought  in habeas and
which may be brought in civil -rights actions, such as (for
state prisoners) suits under 42 U.S.C. 1983.  A claim challenging conditions of confinement , for example,  may be
brought under Section 1983, but a claim alleging unlawfully prolonged imprisonment and seeking immediate or
accelerated release from prison —such as release to parole, as in Preiser itself—must be brought in habeas.

15

B. At least as framed by the court of appeals and the
question presented here,  petitioner’s claim  falls into the
latter category.  Petitioner alleges that BOP has unlawfully withheld First Step Act time credits  that he has
earned, and he seeks as relief a speedier transfer out of
prison and into prerelease custody in a halfway house or
home confinement.   Prerelease custody  in the home or a
community-based facility  differs from prison in fundamental ways, as Congress has repeatedly recognized.  It
is immaterial for habeas purposes that prisoners in prerelease custody  remain in legal custody and remain subject to significant restrictions on their liberty .  The same
is typically true of individuals on parole, yet it is well settled that habeas is available to obtain release from prison
to parole.  “[T]he chief use of habeas corpus has been to
seek the release of persons held in actual, physical custody in prison or jail ,” Jones v. Cunningham, 371 U.S.
236, 238 (1963), and petitioner’s claim fits that bill.   Nor
would there be any other evident home in federal law for
such claims  brought by federal prisoners .  The court of
appeals was plainly wrong to suggest that an implied
right of action under Bivens v. Six Unknown Named
Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics , 403 U.S. 388
(1971), would be an appropriate means for seeking a
transfer from prison to prerelease custody .

“Our legal system  is committed to guaranteeing that
prisoner claims of illegal conduct by their custodians are
fairly handled according to law.”  Perttu v. Richards, 605
U.S. 460, 464 (2025) (brackets and citation omitted).
For decades, prisoner litigation has “account[ed] for an

Ngo, 548 U.S. 81, 94 n.4 (2006).   In response,  Congress

distinguish the domain of federal habeas from that of

repeatedly recognized that habeas is appropriate for a

1. Federal habeas.   “The term habeas corpus  is a generic term ,” Ex parte Bollman , 4 Cranch 75, 84 (1807),
which means  “that you have the body.”  “Over the centuries, a number of writs of habeas corpus evolved at
common law ,” the “most notable” among them being
“habeas corpus ad subjiciendum , often called the ‘Great
Writ.’ ”  Brown v. Davenport , 596 U.S. 118, 128 (2022)
(citation omitted).  The purpose of th at writ was to “ inquire into illegal detention with a view to an order releasing the petitioner .”  Preiser v. Rodriguez , 411 U.S.
475, 484 (1973) (brackets and citation omitted).   If
granted, the  writ issued to the petitioner’s custodian
and ordered the petitioner’s  release from confinement .

J., concurring).
At the Founding, the role of habeas was much narrower than it is today .  The imposition of a  “sentence
after conviction ‘by a court of competent jurisdiction ’
was ‘in itself sufficient cause ’ for a prisoner ’s continued
detention. ”  Jones v. Hendrix, 599 U.S. 465, 483 (2023)
(quoting Davenport , 596 U.S. at 129 ; other citations ,
emphasis, and internal quotation marks omitted).  Among
the writ’s purposes was to secure a pretrial detainee’s
“admission to bail.”  Peyton v. Rowe, 391 U.S. 54, 59
(1968); see Bollman, 4 Cranch at 100.  The Judiciary Act
of 1789, ch. 20, 1 Stat.  73, authorized the federal courts
to grant writs of habeas corpus for federal “prisoners in
gaol.”  § 14, 1 Stat. 82.
“In 1867, Congress expanded the federal courts’ habeas powers to cover ‘all cases where any person ,’ ” including a state prisoner,  “ ‘may be restrained of his or
her liberty in violation of the constitution, or of any

18

treaty or law of the United States. ’ ”  Jones, 599 U.S. at
472-473 (quoting Act of Feb. 5, 1867, ch. 28, 14 Stat. 385).
“[O]ver the years, the writ of habeas corpus evolved as
a remedy available to effect discharge from any confinement contrary to the Constitution or fundamental law,
even though imposed pursuant to conviction by a court
of competent jurisdiction. ”  Preiser, 411 U.S. at 485; see
id. at 485-486.
Congress inaugurated  the modern statutory  framework for federal habeas in 1948.   Act of June 25, 1948,
ch. 646,  §§ 2241 -2255, 62 Stat. 964 -968.  It “ largely recodified the federal courts’ pre -existing habeas authority” in 28 U.S.C. 2241 and 2243, “which, respectively,
confer the power to grant the writ and direct the issuing
court to ‘dispose of the matter as law and justice require.’ ”  Jones, 599 U.S. at 473 (citation omitted) ; see

28 U.S.C. 2255 “as a separate remedial vehicle specifically designed for federal prisoners’ collateral attacks ”
on the validity of their convictions and sentences .  Jones,
599 U.S. at 473.   Unlike a Section 2241  petition, which is
typically filed in the district where the prisoner is confined, a Section 2255 motion to “vacate, set aside or correct the sentence” must be filed in “the court which imposed the sentence.”  28 U.S.C. 2255(a).  But Section 2241
remained the procedural mechanism for a federal prisoner to “ challenge [] ‘the legality of his detention’  without attacking the validity of his sentence .”  Jones, 599
U.S. at 475.   Thus, for instance, a prisoner would use

place or manner not authorized by the sentence ” or

credits. ”  Ibid.; see Brian R. Means, Federal Habeas

C. Petitioner’s Habeas Petition Should Nevertheless Fail
On Other Grounds
Although petitioner’s claim that he is entitled under
the First Step Act to be transferred to a halfway house
or home confinement is cognizable in habeas , it should
not ultimately succeed for at least two reasons.
1. Petitioner failed to exhaust available administrative remedies
First, as the government noted at the petition stage,
petitioner failed to exhaust administrative remedies on
his First Step Act claim.   See Br. in Opp. 8-9.  Both federal and state prisoners alike generally must exhaust
available administrative remedies before seeking habeas relief under Section 2241.  See, e.g., Carmona v.
United States Bureau of Prisons , 243 F.3d 629, 632-634
(2d Cir. 2001) ; Sanchez v. Miller, 792 F.2d 694, 697 (7th
Cir. 1986), cert. denied, 479 U.S. 1056 (1987) .  BOP
maintains an “Administrative Remedy Program ,” which
“allow[s] an inmate to seek formal review of an issue relating to any aspect of his/her own confinement. ”  28
C.F.R. 542.10; see 28 C.F.R. 542.10-542.19.  As both the
magistrate judge and the district court concluded, petitioner invoke d those administrative procedures with respect to some of his claims but not with respect to his
First Step Act claim.  J.A. 24-25, 31-32.  That claim was

36

therefore properly dismissed for lack of exhaustion , irrespective of its cognizability under Section 2241 .
2. Congress has separately barred judicial review  of
BOP’s decision s about where a prisoner is placed
during his term of imprisonment
Second, and o f more general importance, petitioner’s
claim that he must be transferred from prison to prerelease custody is unreviewable under the First Step Act’s
amendment to 18 U.S.C. 3621(b) , which bars judicial review of BOP’s “ designation of a place of imprisonment
under this subsection .”3
a. Section 3621(b) has long vested BOP with broad
discretion,  subject to various statutory considerations ,
to designate the facility in which each federal prisoner
will serve his term of imprisonment.  18 U.S.C. 3621(b) ;
see Tapia v. United States , 564 U.S. 319, 331 (2011) .  “It
is well settled that the decision where to house inmates
is at the core of prison administrators’ expertise.”
McKune v. Lile, 536 U.S. 24, 39 (2002) .
Subject to constitutional constraints, Congress has
“plenary control over the jurisdiction of the federal
courts.”  Trainmen  v. Toledo, Peoria & W. R.R. , 321
U.S. 50, 63 -64 (1944); see U.S. Const. Art. III, § 1.   Congress regularly provides that certain claims may not be
brought under certain judicial -review statutes  or are
not subject to judicial review at all .  See, e.g., Mullin v.
Doe, 146 S. Ct. 2121 (2026).  As noted above, under 18
U.S.C. 3625 , the APA does not apply to BOP’s designation of a place of imprisonment.  In the First Step Act,

And w hen the First Step Act  added Section 3624(g) ,
which governs the application of First Step Act time
credits toward transfer to prerelease custody, it provided that “[t]he time limits” on prerelease custody “under subsections (b) and (c) [of Section 3624] shall not

18 U.S.C. 3624 (c)(2) (limiting home confinement to “ the
shorter of 10 percent of the term of imprisonment of
th[e] prisoner or 6 months ”).  That specific reference to
those time limits  implies that the other conditions on
prerelease custody in Subsection (c), including the express preservation of BOP’s authority under Section
3621 and that statute’s preclusion of judicial review , apply to the placement of a prisoner in prerelease custody
based on First Step Act time credits.   See Esteras v.
United States , 606 U.S. 185, 195 (2025) (applying the
canon “ expressio unius est exclusio alterius ”) (citation
omitted) .  Here, the implication is strengthened because
Congress added the last sentence of Section 3621(b) at
the same time that it enacted Section 3624(g) (10).
By providing that BOP’s “ designation of a place of
imprisonment under this subsection is not reviewable
by any court ,” Section 3621(b) bars prisoners from invoking Section 2241 to challenge BOP’s failure or refusal  to place them in prerelease custody.   18 U.S.C.
3621(b).   And Congress  has specified that such review
is unavailable “[n]otwithstanding any other provision of
law,” ibid., which by its terms makes Section 2241  unavailable .  A notwithstanding (or non obstante ) clause
“shows which of two or more provisions prevails in the
event of a conflict ,” and it “confirms rather than constrains breadth. ”  NLRB v. SW Gen., Inc. , 580 U.S. 288,

Notwithstanding the government’s reading of Section 2241 as including time -credit claims like petitioner’s, Section 3621(b)’s preclusion of habeas review
for such claims does not violate the Suspension Clause,
U.S. Const. Art. I, § 9, Cl. 2 .  The Suspension Clause
protects habeas corpus as it existed “ when the Constitution was drafted and ratified .”  Jones, 599 U.S. at 483
(citation omitted).   Although petitioner’s claim is well
grounded in habeas as the writ has “evolved” over the
centuries,  Preiser, 411 U.S. at 485, it would not have
been cognizable  in habeas at the Founding, when “a sentence after conviction ‘by a court of competent jurisdiction’ was ‘ “in itself sufficient cause ” ’ for a prisoner ’s
continued detention ,” Jones, 599 U.S. at 483  (quoting
Davenport , 596 U.S. at 129)  (emphasis omitted) .  A prisoner’s claim of entitlement to serve his sentence of imprisonment in a particular setting “would have been unrecognizable at that time. ”  Thuraissigiam , 591 U.S. at
107; cf. In re Bonner , 151 U.S. 242 (1894) (granting habeas where the sentencing court lacked jurisdiction to
sentence the defendant to imprisonment).   Section
3621(b)’s preclusion of all judicial review of such claims
therefore presents no Suspension Clause problem.
BOP is of course bound to treat prisoners in accordance with the First Step Act, and frustrated prisoners
may invoke BOP’s procedures for administrative review
of complaints.  But for the reasons set forth above, and
as the Eighth Circuit recently concluded , district courts
lack jurisdiction over suits challenging BOP’s failure to
place prisoners in prerelease custody.   See Osorio-
Calderon  v. Warden, 179 F.4th 1158, 1163-1165 (2026);
see also, e.g., Touzier  v. United States Att’y Gen. , No.

40

21-10761, 2021 WL 3829618, at *2 -*3 (11th Cir. Aug. 27,
2021) (per curiam) .  At the same time that Congress expanded prisoners’ access to prerelease custody in the
First Step Act, it precluded courts from inter vening in
disputes between BOP and prisoners over transfers to
prerelease custody.  “Legislation is, after all, the art of
compromise, the limitations expressed in statutory
terms often the price of passage, and no statute yet
known pursues its stated purpose at all costs.”   Stanley
v. City of Sanford , 606 U.S. 46, 58 (2025) (citation omitted).  The dismissal of petitioner’s habeas petition would
therefore be correct on that ground as well.
D. The Judgment Below Should Be Vacated
Because the court of appeals’ disposition of this case
was correct on the other grounds  just discussed , this
Court could affirm the judgment below.  See Upper
Skagit Indian Tribe v. Lundgren , 584 U.S. 554, 560
(2018) (“we have discretion to affirm on any ground supported by the law and the record that will not expand
the relief granted below”).  But the government acknowledges that the Court’s “usual practice”  in these circumstances  would be to vacate the judgment and remand
for consideration of those issues in the first instance  by
the courts below.  E.M.D. Sales, Inc. v. Carrera, 604 U.S.
45, 54 (2025).   This Court is “ a court of review, not of
first view .”  Cutter v. Wilkinson , 544 U.S. 709, 718 n.7
(2005).
Moreover, the question whether Section 3621(b)’s review bar applies to time-credit claims like petitioner’s
will be one of broad importance , but it is not otherwise
ripe for  this Court’s review.  It has thus far been addressed in only one precedential court of appeals decision, which was decided after th e grant of certiorari in
this case.   See Osorio-Calderon , supra.

of certiorari as improvidently granted.   For the reasons
